# Summary of Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was a pioneering computer scientist and electrical engineer known for her revolutionary contributions to very-large-scale integration (VLSI) chip design. After beginning her education at MIT in the 1950s and an early career at IBM Research working on the Advanced Computing Systems project, she underwent a gender transition in 1968, after which IBM fired her for revealing her plans. She later received a public apology from IBM and was honored with a Lifetime Achievement Award in 2020.
Post-transition, Conway restarted her career stealthily, working at Memorex and then joining Xerox PARC, where she led the LSI Systems group and co-developed the Mead–Conway VLSI design methodology alongside Carver Mead. She invented essential concepts such as scalable design rules and the multiproject wafer (MPW) technology, contributing substantially to chip design as a field, influencing academia and industry, and fostering the rise of the electronic design automation industry. Conway also helped develop the MOSIS prototyping system and taught a seminal VLSI design course at MIT in 1978. She later worked at DARPA and the University of Michigan until retiring as professor emerita. Recognized for her transformative impact, she coined the “Conway effect,” highlighting the systematic overlooking of underrepresented innovators.
Conway was a prominent transgender rights activist, sharing her personal story publicly from 1999 onwards, advocating for trans inclusion in tech fields and broader social acceptance. She assisted many transgender individuals and was involved in campaigns against controversial trans-related typologies. Her numerous awards include IEEE Fellow, membership in the National Academy of Engineering, the Computer Pioneer Award, and honorary doctorates from several institutions. In 2024, she passed away due to a heart condition at age 86.
